summary: Adds enhancements to the Constrained Application Protocol that reduce security problems in some use cases. The Echo option lets a server check that a request is fresh or that a client really can be reached at its claimed address. The Request-Tag option lets a server match block-wise fragments of the same request. It also updates RFC 7252 on handling of tokens.

plainLanguage.summary: A server can ask a client to repeat a secret word to prove it is really there, and labels the pieces of a long message so they are not mixed up.

questions: what is the coap echo option
what is the coap request-tag option
how does coap prevent amplification attacks
why must coap tokens not be reused
subtitle: Two CoAP options that prove a request is fresh and keep block-wise fragments apart, plus tighter Token rules.

tldr.problem: CoAP servers cannot tell when a request was sent, block-wise fragments from different bodies can be mixed up, and Token reuse can make a client match a response to the wrong request.
tldr.mechanism: The Echo option is a server challenge that the client repeats to prove freshness or reachability. The Request-Tag option labels the blocks of one request body. Clients must not reuse Tokens in ways that risk wrong matches.
tldr.outcome: The RFC updates RFC 7252 so servers SHOULD use Echo against amplification attacks and clients follow stricter Token rules when CoAP is secured.

facts.label: Safe default first response
facts.value: 136 bytes or less in CoAP serialization

today: RFC 9175 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2022 and it updates RFC 7252. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why CoAP Needs These Additions
sections.content:
The first CoAP specifications (RFC 7252, RFC 7641 and RFC 7959) assumed security could be provided on a separate layer such as DTLS. For some use cases that is not enough, so this document adds two options, Echo and Request-Tag.

The options do not replace a security protocol. They define data that gives extra security features when integrity protected by DTLS, TLS or OSCORE. The RFC also updates RFC 7252 in two ways: servers are recommended to use Echo against amplification attacks, and the Token processing rules for clients become stricter.
sections.plainLanguage: Locking the door is not always enough. These additions are extra checks that work together with the lock.

sections.title: Request Freshness and the Echo Option
sections.content:
A CoAP server generally cannot verify when a request was sent, even if it is protected with DTLS. That makes requests open to delay attacks, which are especially dangerous for actuators. Running a DTLS handshake for each request is usually too costly for constrained environments, and with proxies it says nothing about when the client made the request.

The Echo option is a lightweight challenge-response. The server puts an opaque value in a response, and the client echoes it back in a later request. The option is elective, safe to forward, not part of the cache key and not repeatable. Its option number is 252 and its value is 1 to 40 bytes. Clients and intermediaries MUST treat the value as opaque.

The server decides which requests must be fresh. If a request has to be fresh and has no valid Echo value, the server MUST NOT process it further and SHOULD answer 4.01 (Unauthorized) with an Echo option. The client SHOULD then resend the request with that value. A client MUST only send Echo values back to the endpoint it got them from.
sections.plainLanguage: The server says, 'Tell me this secret word to show you are really asking right now.' The client repeats the word, and the server knows the request is not an old one being replayed.

sections.title: How Echo Checks Freshness
sections.content:
The server can bind the Echo value to a point in time and check that t1 - t0 < T, where t1 is when the request arrived and t0 is when the value was generated. This is time-based freshness. It can instead cache a value tied to events, so a request is fresh if no new event happened since the value was issued. This is event-based freshness.

When Echo serves freshness, client aliveness or state synchronization, the value MUST be integrity protected between the endpoints, for example by DTLS, TLS or an OSCORE Inner option. A server may also send a preemptive Echo value with a successful response, so the client can prove freshness in a later request without an extra round trip.

Proxies have their own rules. A CoAP-to-CoAP proxy MAY set Echo on responses, but it MUST make sure the client's request was generated after the Echo value it used towards the server was first seen. An HTTP-to-CoAP proxy that cannot establish freshness MUST NOT repeat an unsafe request and SHOULD respond with 503 (Service Unavailable).
sections.plainLanguage: The server either checks that the secret word was given out only a moment ago, or checks that nothing important has happened since it gave the word out.

sections.title: Uses of Echo and Amplification Mitigation
sections.content:
The RFC lists four applications of Echo. Actuation requests may need freshness guarantees, and all unsafe methods such as POST, PUT and DELETE may need them. A server can synchronize state or time with a client, as long as the client is the authority for that property. An attacker can spoof a victim's address on a request that triggers a large response, and Echo can verify the source address first. A server can also check that a client is alive.

The amplification factor is the ratio between the size of the request and the total size of the responses. The RFC points out that a factor of 3 is considered acceptable for unconstrained applications in RFC 9000, and gives a safe default of initial responses no larger than 136 bytes in CoAP serialization. An Echo response sent for this purpose MUST be piggybacked or Non-confirmable, never separate, because retransmission would cause amplification.

Section 2.6 formally updates RFC 7252: a CoAP server SHOULD mitigate amplification by answering unauthenticated clients with 4.01 (Unauthorized) and an Echo option.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine someone shouting your name at a loudspeaker so it blasts you with noise. Asking 'is this really you?' with a tiny message first stops the loudspeaker from being tricked.

sections.title: Request-Tag and Block-Wise Transfers
sections.content:
Block-wise transfer (RFC 7959) sends a large body as a sequence of blocks using the Block1 and Block2 options. It cannot detect blocks swapped between different bodies sent to the same resource with the same block number, even with DTLS or OSCORE inside the replay window. An attacker could replace a later operation's blocks with an earlier operation's blocks.

The Request-Tag option identifies request bodies, similar to ETag but short-lived and set by the client. It is elective, safe to forward, repeatable and part of the cache key. Its option number is 292 and its value is 0 to 8 bytes. It is used only in requests and MUST NOT be present in responses.

For body integrity, exchanges MUST be integrity protected end to end, and the client MUST NOT recycle a request tag in a new matchable operation until the previous one has concluded. Request-Tag also allows concurrent block-wise operations on one resource, which is useful for proxies. For response bodies, a server MUST use Block2 together with ETag and MUST NOT use one ETag value for different representations.
sections.plainLanguage: When you send a long letter in pieces, you write the same label on every piece. The receiver can then put the right pieces together, even if pieces from two different letters arrive in the same week.

sections.title: Token Processing for Request-Response Binding
sections.content:
A client must be able to bind a response to the request it made. Otherwise it may accept an old response or one for another resource: a request for GET /status might be matched with a stale answer of 'on' instead of 'off'. HTTP/1.1 gets this from ordered, reliable delivery. In CoAP, concurrent requests are told apart by their Token, and RFC 7252 only says Tokens in use SHOULD be unique.

The RFC adds text to the Token rules: when CoAP is used with a security protocol that does not bind requests to responses, such as DTLS or TLS, the client MUST make sure Tokens are not used so that a response risks matching the wrong request. One easy way is to use a sequence number as the Token, starting at zero for each new or rekeyed secure connection, and this SHOULD be followed. The rules for servers are not changed. Responses that are cryptographically bound to requests, as in OSCORE, can reuse Tokens indefinitely.
sections.plainLanguage: When you ask many questions at once, you number them. The rule is to never reuse a number while an old answer might still show up, or you could match an answer to the wrong question.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Notes
sections.content:
Echo values should be unpredictable. If a value is guessable, a request could be built ahead of time. When uniqueness is based on randomness, the value SHOULD contain 64 (pseudo)random bits that nobody but the server can predict. Servers SHOULD use a monotonic clock for timestamps, because moving a non-monotonic clock backward would make the server accept expired values.

Implementations SHOULD NOT put privacy-sensitive data in Echo or Request-Tag values. Unencrypted timestamps can reveal server details such as location or time since reboot. Like HTTP cookies, Echo could be abused for tracking, especially preemptive values, so servers MUST NOT use it to correlate requests for anything other than freshness and reachability. Where proxies terminate (D)TLS, the security claims hold only if all intermediaries are fully trusted.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret word should be hard to guess and should not give away anything about who you are. It also should not be used to keep track of you.

sections.title: Registered Options and Echo Values
sections.content:
IANA added two entries to the CoAP Option Numbers registry: 252 for Echo and 292 for Request-Tag, both referencing RFC 9175.

The content of an Echo value is up to the server. Appendix A outlines three ways to generate it: a list of cached random values with timestamps (RECOMMENDED in general), an integrity-protected timestamp (RECOMMENDED when Echo is encrypted between client and server), and a persistent counter, which suits only cases where the client is the authority over the synchronized property.
sections.plainLanguage: The two new options got official numbers in a public list. The server can create its secret words in several ways, each with its own trade-offs.
